summary: India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites as of October 2026: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. The first four, Agra Fort, the Taj Mahal, Ajanta and Ellora, were inscribed in 1983. The newest is the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh, inscribed in July 2026 at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee.

sections.h2: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in India?
paras: As of October 2026, India has 45 sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Of these, 37 are cultural, 7 are natural and 1, Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim, is mixed, recognised for both natural and cultural value. India has one of the larger national totals on the list.

The pace of inscription has picked up in recent years. Dholavira and the Ramappa temple were added in 2021, Santiniketan and the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas in 2023, the Moidams of the Ahom dynasty in 2024, the Maratha Military Landscapes of India in 2025 and the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath in July 2026, at the World Heritage Committee's 48th session in Busan.

paras: The table lists all 45 sites in order of inscription. Where a site was extended later, the later years are given in brackets. Sites spread across more than one state are listed with each state.

paras: The oldest evidence on the list is at Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, where rock shelters hold paintings from many periods and a long record of human use. Our walk on [Bhimbetka's painted shelters](bhimbetka-painted-shelters-and-prehistoric-landscapes.html) explains how the layers of paintings are read. Dholavira in Kachchh, Gujarat, is the only Harappan city on the list, known for its water reservoirs, its divided city plan and a large inscription in the Indus script. A [visit to Dholavira](dholavira-harappan-urbanism-in-kachchh.html) shows how a city was built for a dry climate.

Buddhist heritage is well represented. Sanchi has stupas from the Mauryan period onwards and carved gateways of around the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE. The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya marks the place of the Buddha's enlightenment, Nalanda preserves the remains of a great monastic university, and Sarnath, inscribed in 2026, is where the Buddha is said to have given his first sermon. The [Sanchi visit](sanchi-stupas-gateways-and-buddhist-art.html) and the [Nalanda programme](nalanda-monastic-university-landscape.html) cover two of these in depth.

Rock-cut architecture appears at Ajanta, with its Buddhist paintings; Ellora, with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves side by side; and Elephanta, with its great 6th century Shiva cave in Mumbai harbour. Our [Elephanta visit](elephanta-shiva-and-rock-cut-architecture.html) is an easy day out from Mumbai.

Temple sites cover most of the regional styles explained in our guide to [Indian temple architecture](indian-temple-architecture.html): Pallava monuments at Mahabalipuram, the Chalukya temples of Pattadakal, the Chandela temples of Khajuraho, the Sun Temple at Konark, the Great Living Chola Temples at Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram, the Kakatiya temple at Ramappa, and the Hoysala temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura.

Delhi has three World Heritage Sites: the Qutb Minar and its monuments, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort Complex. Agra adds the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort, and Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's short-lived capital, lies nearby. Hampi preserves the capital of the Vijayanagara empire, and Champaner-Pavagadh in Gujarat a 15th and 16th century sultanate city with its mosques and fortifications.

Defensive architecture is represented by the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan (Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer) and the Maratha Military Landscapes of India, a group of twelve forts in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu including Gingee. The living historic cities on the list are Ahmadabad and Jaipur. The Moidams of Assam are different again: a royal burial landscape of the Ahom kings at Charaideo. See also our explainer on [forts of India](forts-of-india.html).

Some of India's World Heritage Sites are less than five hundred years old. The Churches and Convents of Old Goa date from the Portuguese period. Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus in Mumbai, completed in 1888, and the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai record a colonial port city and its 20th century growth. Our [Mumbai Art Deco and Victorian Gothic walk](mumbai-art-deco-and-victorian-gothic-walk.html) covers the Oval Maidan ensemble.

The Mountain Railways of India, the Darjeeling Himalayan, Nilgiri and Kalka-Shimla lines, are working railways. Jantar Mantar in Jaipur is an 18th century observatory. Santiniketan in West Bengal, founded around Rabindranath Tagore's school and university, and the Capitol Complex in Chandigarh, designed by Le Corbusier, are 20th century additions.

sections.h2: Natural World Heritage Sites in India
paras: India's seven natural sites protect very different ecosystems. Kaziranga and Manas in Assam are known for the one-horned rhinoceros, tigers and grasslands. Keoladeo in Rajasthan is a wetland famous for birds. The Sundarbans in West Bengal is the largest mangrove forest in the world, shared with Bangladesh. Nanda Devi and the Valley of Flowers in Uttarakhand and the Great Himalayan National Park in Himachal Pradesh protect high mountain habitats. The Western Ghats, inscribed as a series of protected areas across several states, is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots.

Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim is India's only mixed site: its glaciers and forests are of natural value, and the mountain and its landscape are sacred in the Buddhist and indigenous traditions of Sikkim.

sections.h2: What does UNESCO World Heritage inscription mean?
paras: The World Heritage List was created under the 1972 World Heritage Convention, which India ratified in 1977. A site is inscribed by the World Heritage Committee if it is judged to have 'outstanding universal value' under at least one of ten criteria, and if it meets standards of integrity, authenticity and protection.

Inscription does not transfer ownership or management to UNESCO. The site remains the responsibility of the national government, in India usually the Archaeological Survey of India, state governments or forest departments. What changes is international attention: India reports on the site's condition, the Committee can raise concerns, and a site under serious threat can be placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Our explainer on [heritage conservation in India](heritage-conservation-in-india.html) covers what protection involves on the ground.

sections.h2: India's tentative list and how sites are nominated
paras: Before a site can be nominated, it must be on the country's Tentative List, a public inventory of places the government considers suitable. India's Tentative List contains dozens of cultural and natural properties, and new proposals were added in 2026. From this list, the government prepares a detailed nomination dossier, usually for one site a year, which is assessed by advisory bodies (ICOMOS for cultural sites, IUCN for natural ones) before the Committee decides.

The process takes years and involves mapping boundaries, preparing management plans and consulting local communities. Some sites are inscribed on first attempt; others are referred back or deferred for more work.

sections.h2: Visiting UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India with a group
paras: Many of the sites are clustered, which makes group trips practical. Delhi, Agra and Jaipur together hold eight World Heritage Sites, and our [Three capitals journey](three-capitals-delhi-agra-and-jaipur.html) and [Golden Triangle with an archaeologist](the-golden-triangle-with-an-archaeologist.html) are built around them. Central India has Sanchi, Bhimbetka and Khajuraho within reach of Bhopal, covered in our [Central India journey](central-india-rock-art-and-buddhist-archaeology.html). Mumbai has three, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco ensembles and Elephanta.

For schools and colleges, a site visit works best with a short lecture beforehand and a focused question on the day. Check the ASI or the site's official website before you go for current timings, tickets and photography rules, since these change. Talaash Heritage can arrange visits with an archaeologist or historian at many of these sites, or build a [study tour for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html) around a region.

faq.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in India in 2026?
faq.a: India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites as of October 2026: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. The 45th is the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh, inscribed in July 2026.

faq.q: Which is the latest UNESCO World Heritage Site in India?
faq.a: The latest is the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh, inscribed in July 2026 at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan. Before that came the Maratha Military Landscapes of India in 2025.

faq.q: Which were the first UNESCO sites in India?
faq.a: India's first four World Heritage Sites were inscribed in 1983: Agra Fort, the Taj Mahal, Ajanta Caves and Ellora Caves.

faq.q: Which state has the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites?
faq.a: Maharashtra has the most when sites shared with other states are counted, including Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Mumbai ensembles, the Maratha Military Landscapes and part of the Western Ghats. Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Karnataka also have several.

faq.q: What is the only mixed World Heritage Site in India?
faq.a: Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim, inscribed in 2016, is India's only mixed site. It is recognised both for its mountain ecosystems and for the cultural and sacred meaning of the mountain and its landscape.

faq.q: How many natural World Heritage Sites does India have?
faq.a: Seven: Kaziranga National Park, Keoladeo National Park, Manas Wildlife Sanctuary, Sundarbans National Park, Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers National Parks, the Western Ghats and the Great Himalayan National Park Conservation Area.

faq.q: Who looks after UNESCO sites in India?
faq.a: The Indian government does. Most cultural sites are managed by the Archaeological Survey of India or state departments, and natural sites by forest departments. UNESCO monitors their condition through reports and the World Heritage Committee but does not manage them.

faq.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in Delhi?
faq.a: Delhi has three: the Qutb Minar and its monuments, Humayun's Tomb, both inscribed in 1993, and the Red Fort Complex, inscribed in 2007.
